questions.question: What information describes a nonzero complex number in polar form?
What does the modulus $r$ measure in polar coordinates?
options: The angle from the positive real axis
The sign of the real part

questions.question: Why is the polar angle not unique?
options: The modulus can be any complex number.
Sine and cosine are not used in polar form.

questions.question: What is special about the polar angle of the zero complex number?
options: It is not uniquely determined when $r=0$.
It is fixed by the real part.

questions.question: What does polar form separate that Cartesian form combines as real and imaginary parts?
What is the modulus of $3+4\mathrm i$?
Which polar data describe $1+\mathrm i$?
What complex number is represented by $2(\cos\pi+\mathrm i\sin\pi)$?
Which two polar descriptions represent the same nonzero complex number?
If $r=0$ in $r(\cos\varphi+\mathrm i\sin\varphi)$, what complex number is represented?
Why is the convention $r\ge0$ useful in polar form?
options: It makes every complex number real.
It keeps the modulus as a distance, while angle records direction.
It forces every argument to be unique without further convention.

questions.question: Why is polar form especially useful for complex multiplication?
options: It turns multiplication into adding moduli and multiplying angles.
It turns multiplication into multiplying moduli and adding angles.
It avoids using the imaginary unit.

questions.question: How does Cartesian form differ from polar form for the same complex number?
options: Cartesian form applies only to real numbers.
Polar form has no connection with the complex plane, regardless of the specific input chosen.
Polar form replaces complex numbers by matrices.
Cartesian form uses real and imaginary coordinates; polar form uses distance and angle.

questions.question: Evaluate $2(\cos(\pi/2)+\mathrm i\sin(\pi/2))$.
Which polar description represents $-1$?
Which expression has the same value as $2(\cos(\pi/3)+\mathrm i\sin(\pi/3))$?
What does choosing a principal argument try to fix?
options: The fact that moduli are negative.
The impossibility of writing complex numbers in polar form.
The need for a real and imaginary part.
The non-uniqueness caused by angles differing by multiples of $2\pi$.

questions.question: Why is it risky to say “the argument” of a nonzero complex number without a convention?
options: Because there are infinitely many arguments differing by $2\pi k$.
Because the modulus also has infinitely many values.
Because the complex number must be zero.
Because sine and cosine have no periods.

questions.question: Find polar data for $-\sqrt3+\mathrm i$ using $0\le\varphi \lt 2\pi$.
What complex number is represented by $\sqrt2(\cos(-\pi/4)+\mathrm i\sin(-\pi/4))$?
